publicationRule: Worked examples illustrate reasoning paths, not universal prescriptions. Keep numerical values contextual, preserve uncertainty, and do not publish an example as an authoritative answer key until independent review is recorded.

examples.title: VPD reading looks acceptable, leaves still show excessive demand
examples.scenario: A room controller reports a VPD inside the facility's preferred operating band, but upper-canopy leaves are curling upward and leaf temperature differs from the controller's assumed value.
reasoningPath: Treat the controller value as a calculated description of the measured air, not proof that every leaf experiences the same vapor-pressure conditions.
Verify the air-temperature and RH sensors, then measure representative leaf temperature and compare multiple canopy positions.
Check airflow, light load, root-zone water status, and duration of the excursion because each can change leaf response without changing the room-average display.
Recalculate leaf-referenced VPD using measured leaf temperature when that is the question being tested.
Change one primary environmental driver at a time where safe, then re-measure both environment and plant response.
evidenceToCollect: air temperature and RH at canopy height
weakAnswerPatterns: The VPD number is in range, so the environment cannot be the cause.
Raise humidity immediately without checking sensor placement or leaf temperature.
Treat one chart band as a universal target for every cultivar and stage.
examples.verification: A stronger conclusion requires representative canopy measurements and a repeatable improvement in plant response after the targeted change, not merely a corrected controller number.
examples.boundary: No universal Cannabis VPD target is implied; cultivar, stage, leaf temperature, disease risk, root status, and measurement method affect interpretation.

examples.title: High center PPFD, weak edge growth
examples.scenario: A grow reports strong PPFD directly under the center of each fixture, yet edge plants stretch and yield less.
reasoningPath: Reject the single-point measurement as a description of whole-canopy light distribution.
Create a repeatable PPFD grid at a defined canopy plane and record fixture height, spacing, dimming, and measurement geometry.
Calculate distribution metrics and inspect the actual minimums/hotspots instead of relying on the average alone.
Compare light pattern with plant height, morphology, leaf temperature, and final zone-by-zone outcomes.
Adjust fixture layout, height, dimming, or canopy geometry only after identifying the spatial problem.
weakAnswerPatterns: The fixture is powerful enough because the center reading is high.
Use one average PPFD value to describe uniformity.
Raise intensity everywhere without checking hotspots.
examples.verification: Repeat the same mapped measurements after the adjustment and compare edge-to-center uniformity plus plant response.
examples.boundary: Uniformity targets depend on crop geometry, fixture design, production goal, and the chosen metric; one map should not be generalized to all rooms.

examples.title: Yellowing appears after a bloom-booster increase
examples.scenario: Lower leaves yellow after phosphorus-heavy bloom inputs are increased. The grower assumes phosphorus deficiency and proposes adding more.
reasoningPath: Separate the visible symptom from the nutrient diagnosis because lower-leaf yellowing is not phosphorus-specific.
Review root-zone pH/EC, irrigation pattern, root condition, recent recipe changes, and the broader symptom distribution.
Check whether the nutrient change increased total ionic strength or antagonism risk rather than assuming the named nutrient is missing.
Compare feed and root-zone context over time instead of interpreting a single runoff value as proof.
Only change the nutrient program after competing root-zone and environmental explanations are evaluated.
evidenceToCollect: feed/root-zone pH and EC with sampling method
weakAnswerPatterns: Yellow lower leaves mean phosphorus deficiency.
More bloom booster is the safest first response.
A single runoff number proves the nutrient cause.
examples.verification: New growth and root-zone trends should improve after the targeted correction without creating a new imbalance.
examples.boundary: This example does not prescribe a phosphorus target or fertilizer rate; diagnosis depends on system, substrate, stage, sampling, and product formulation.

examples.title: One photo is labeled a nutrient deficiency
examples.scenario: A single close-up photo shows yellow and necrotic leaf tissue. The initial claim is 'magnesium deficiency.'
reasoningPath: Describe the symptom before naming the cause: tissue age, location, pattern, progression, and affected fraction.
Request whole-plant and crop-context evidence, then compare affected and unaffected plants.
Inspect roots and irrigation delivery and review pH/EC, environment, recent changes, pests, disease signs, and chemical exposure.
Keep multiple plausible causes until a measurement or sample discriminates among them.
Define what observation after correction would support or weaken the leading hypothesis.
weakAnswerPatterns: Leaf color alone identifies the deficiency.
The most common cause must be correct.
Improvement after several simultaneous changes proves the diagnosis.
examples.verification: A strong diagnosis predicts the spatial/temporal pattern and survives comparison with competing explanations, then is supported by a defined response after a controlled correction.
examples.boundary: Some cases remain multifactorial or unresolved and may require laboratory or specialist confirmation.

examples.title: Recurring pest problem despite calendar sprays
examples.scenario: A facility applies a pesticide on a fixed schedule, but the same pest keeps returning in the same production zone.
reasoningPath: Treat repeated recurrence as a systems problem rather than automatically escalating spray frequency.
Confirm pest identity and life stage, map hotspots, and review intake, movement, sanitation, exclusion, crop residues, and environmental conditions.
Identify which prevention barrier is failing and whether the intervention timing matches pest biology.
Check legal label requirements, resistance-management considerations, and compatibility with biological controls.
Use repeated counts and defined thresholds/tolerances to decide whether the revised program is working.
weakAnswerPatterns: Spray more often because the product did not work.
Seeing fewer adults once proves control.
IPM is just rotating pesticides.
examples.verification: The revised program should reduce pest pressure over repeated scouting intervals while preserving compliance and preventing the same pathway from reseeding the problem.
examples.boundary: No pesticide, threshold, release rate, or treatment interval is prescribed here; lawful use depends on current labels, jurisdiction, crop context, and facility policy.

examples.title: Small F2 population misses a rare trait combination
examples.scenario: A breeder expects to recover several independent favorable traits in an F2 but only grows a small population and finds none.
reasoningPath: Translate the desired phenotype into an explicit genetic/trait model instead of assuming one plant should appear by chance.
Estimate how trait number, linkage, dominance, recombination, penetrance, and scoring error affect recovery probability.
Set population size from the probability of the desired combination and the need for multiple independent candidates.
Preserve all scored classes and environmental context so absence can be interpreted rather than hidden by selection.
Revise the population design if the probability of recovery was too low for the chosen sample size.
weakAnswerPatterns: No selected plant means the trait combination is impossible.
A small F2 is enough if the parents are strong.
Only the best plants need to be recorded.
examples.verification: A defensible conclusion compares observed counts with a predeclared model and acknowledges when population size cannot distinguish rarity from absence.
examples.boundary: Simple Mendelian probabilities apply only when the underlying assumptions are justified; quantitative traits and linkage can change expected recovery sharply.

examples.title: New meter shows more decimal places
examples.scenario: A replacement meter displays two decimal places instead of one, and the team concludes that measurements are now more accurate.
reasoningPath: Separate display resolution from accuracy, precision, repeatability, bias, and uncertainty.
Check manufacturer specifications, calibration/verification records, reference standards, and repeat measurements.
Compare the instrument against a suitable reference across the actual operating range.
Document as-found condition and any adjustment rather than assuming calibration erases all uncertainty.
Report only the digits justified by method performance and decision needs.
weakAnswerPatterns: More decimal places always mean more accuracy.
A recent calibration guarantees every future result.
Repeat readings close together prove the result is true.
examples.verification: The instrument must meet predefined acceptance criteria against appropriate references and demonstrate suitable repeatability over the intended range.
examples.boundary: Measurement uncertainty is method- and use-specific; this example does not establish a universal tolerance.

examples.title: One sensor is used to represent an entire room
examples.scenario: A cultivation room uses one centrally located sensor to support a claim that all plants experienced the same temperature and RH.
reasoningPath: Define the population and decision: whether the claim concerns the whole room, canopy zones, time periods, or a specific crop operation.
Identify likely spatial and temporal gradients created by fixtures, walls, doors, airflow, irrigation, and canopy density.
Choose representative sampling locations and times before collecting the data.
Distinguish repeated readings from one sensor from independent spatial samples.
Use the resulting variation to decide whether one fixed sensor is representative enough for the intended decision.
weakAnswerPatterns: A central sensor automatically represents the room.
Many readings from one location equal many independent samples.
An average proves there were no harmful extremes.
examples.verification: A representative plan should reproduce the important spatial and temporal variation well enough to support the stated decision, with limits documented.
examples.boundary: Sampling density depends on room geometry, variability, equipment, risk, and the consequence of missing extremes.
